purpose: Chlorpromazine is used to treat conditions like schizophrenia, severe anxiety, and bipolar disorder. It can also help control nausea, vomiting, and hiccups that won't go away. Sometimes it is used before surgery to help you relax or to manage agitation.
how_it_works: Your brain uses chemical messengers called dopamine and serotonin to send signals. In conditions like schizophrenia, these signals can become overactive and cause symptoms like hallucinations or confused thinking. Chlorpromazine works by blocking certain dopamine receptors in the brain, which helps calm those overactive signals and reduce symptoms.
common_side_effects: Drowsiness or feeling sleepy, dizziness when standing up quickly, dry mouth, blurry vision, constipation, weight gain, sensitivity to sunlight, and feeling restless or having muscle stiffness. Some people may notice their skin looks slightly gray or tan with long-term use.
warnings: This medicine can cause a serious condition called tardive dyskinesia — uncontrolled movements of the face or body — especially with long-term use. It may also cause a rare but dangerous reaction called neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which includes high fever and muscle rigidity — seek emergency help immediately if this happens. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication. Do not drive until you know how it affects you. Older adults with dementia should use this medication with caution as it may increase risk of stroke or death.
typical_dosing: Doses vary widely depending on what it is being used for. For adults with psychiatric conditions, starting doses are often 25–50 mg taken 3 times a day, and your doctor may slowly increase the dose as needed. For nausea or hiccups, lower doses are usually used. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribes and never stop suddenly without talking to your doctor first.
